panels.description: Wide, full page width. Memory, in dry ochre tones unlike anything else in the chapter: a Deccan hill fort on black rock, a thick bastion, cannon ports, lime-washed walls under a hard sun. No figure close enough to identify.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: In the Deccan, a kingdom revealed itself in its forts.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: You could stand on a bastion and read a ruler's mind in stone and mortar.

panels.description: Morning in Travancore, full wet green. The door of Nagoji's quarters on the estate where he lodges: laterite walls, a tiled roof still dripping from the night's rain, coconut palms. Nagoji (commander sheet: rust-red turban, cream tunic, broad red sash, cream trousers, boots, talwar; thick curled moustache, CLEAN-SHAVEN CHIN, small gold ear stud, long curly hair gathered under the turban; no beard) stepping out, still settling his sash. Ramayyan already waiting on the path: thin, sharp fine features, receding hair, plain white cloth without a speck of dust, a bundle of palm leaves under one arm.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: In Travancore, I learned, you had to listen in different places.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Ramayyan taught me that, though he never called it teaching.

panels.description: Two-shot, medium. Ramayyan has already turned to go. Nagoji one step behind, following.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: Walk with me, Sawant.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: When the diwan of a kingdom tells you to walk, you do not ask where.

panels.description: Wide. A small temple on a hill above a cluster of houses and pepper gardens. Its gateway is a modest Kerala one: a low laterite base and a two-tiered sloping tiled roof on wooden posts, no tall stone tower. Stone steps worn hollow in the centre. At the foot of the steps, Nagoji's boots stand side by side with his talwar laid across them. Ramayyan and Nagoji climbing barefoot; villagers, men and women, stepping aside for Ramayyan, and he gives each one the same small nod.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: A temple to Ayyappa, the forest warrior. Patron of all who carried arms in these hills.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Every greeting, Ramayyan put away somewhere behind his eyes.

panels.description: The outer courtyard. Oil lamps, bells on chains, incense smoke winding round stone pillars, Brahmins at their rituals in the background. Deep in the sanctum doorway, small and lit from below, the officiating priest holds a lamp tray: gold-bordered mundu, sacred thread, forehead marks, hair in a knot. In the foreground, at the innermost threshold, Ramayyan has stopped and turned back to face Nagoji: receding hair, plain unbordered white cloth over both shoulders, no forehead marks. Both men barefoot; Nagoji without boots or talwar.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: You do not have to go closer. The god knows you have your own ways.

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: Gods and I have an understanding. I try not to waste their time.

panels.description: In the shade of the mandapa. Ramayyan and Nagoji side by side, barefoot, the sanctum's lamp glow ahead of them, the bright courtyard behind. The faintest smile on Ramayyan.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: Watch instead.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: Who pays for the oil in those lamps?

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: The temple. From offerings.

panels.description: Nagoji in close profile, thinking: thick curled moustache, clean-shaven chin, small gold ear stud, rust-red turban. Three small insets along the top edge, drawn inside this panel's own frame, showing what he is seeing in his head: boys at practice in a kalari, women sorting pepper on mats, a bullock cart groaning under sacks of paddy.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN (off)
copy.text: Where do the offerings come from?

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: From the fields. From houses like Padmini Amma's.

panels.description: Ramayyan, turned toward the sanctum, counting on his fingers. Above him, an old dark water stain on the stone of the mandapa roof.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: And who pays when the temple roof leaks? When the priest demands new ornaments for the god? When the elephant that carries the idol in procession goes lame?

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: The king. If he is wise.

panels.description: Close on Ramayyan. Lamplight in his eyes.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: If he wants men to believe the god favours his reign.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: A temple is not just stone. It is a ledger. Offerings in. Blessings out.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: The names written on both sides matter.

panels.description: Wide, the largest panel on the page. A courtyard wall set with dozens of small niches, a lamp burning in every one. Below it, worshippers from landed Nair houses: a woman of a landed house with her attendants, an older man in a white mundu. Beyond them, through the open outer gateway and outside the temple wall, a fisherman and a bare-shouldered labourer hand a small pot of oil across the threshold to a temple servant; they do not step inside. Ramayyan and Nagoji small at the edge of the frame, in shadow, barefoot.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN (off)
copy.text: Each of those lamps is paid for by a house.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN (off)
copy.text: When the king asks for extra tax to pay for muskets and forts, they remember whether he feeds their god.

panels.description: Wide establishing. Awnings of cloth and palm leaves. Traders from the interior haggling over sacks of rice and jars of oil. On a raised platform, an Arab merchant in a flowing white robe sits cross-legged, weighing silver coins on a small brass scale while his servant counts sacks of pepper. Beside a cloth stall, a young Syrian Christian scribe (clean-shaven, black hair, white cloth, small wooden cross) at a low desk, writing, a stack of folded paper bills at his elbow. Marakkar men bargaining over pepper and cardamom, their eyes flicking toward a path that runs down to the water. Ramayyan and Nagoji, boots and talwar back on, entering at the edge.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Silver chuckrams. Pepper by the candi, the measure by which fortunes were made or lost on this coast.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: And hundis, that could turn pepper in Travancore into gold in Muscat without a single coin crossing the sea.

panels.description: Two-shot. Nagoji unimpressed. Ramayyan's eyes already somewhere down the row of stalls.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: Do you see the pattern?

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: I see men arguing over coins. That is the same everywhere.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: Look closer.

panels.description: The cloth stall from 3.1: a table piled with cloth, pepper sacks stacked behind it. Yusuf Marakkar, a sea captain: tall and lean, white skullcap, neatly trimmed dark beard, no scar, short coat over a white tunic, leaning across the table toward the stallholder. At the end of the table, the young Syrian Christian scribe from 3.1, writing on paper.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Yusuf. Ibrahim's cousin, from the coastal hall.

copy.speaker: YUSUF
copy.text: If your pepper is worm eaten, my mast will refuse to carry it. The Dutch will not pay for rot.

panels.description: The stallholder: a woman in her late twenties, a baby slung on her hip, arms folded. Plain undyed cotton mundu with a cloth over the shoulder, no gold, no jasmine, hair in a simple knot. Immovable.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Not much older than Revathi Bayi.

copy.speaker: WOMAN
copy.text: My pepper has fewer worms than your honesty.

copy.speaker: WOMAN
copy.text: Your ships carry news as well as goods. When you bring Dutch coins into our land, remember that the king counts them with his fingers, not yours.

panels.description: Yusuf mid-laugh, his eyes cut sideways to one target: a pale-faced Dutch factor sitting small in the mid-background further down the market, in 1740s dress (long-skirted dark coat with deep cuffs, waistcoat, knee breeches, stockings, black tricorne; a trader, not a blue-coated soldier). In the foreground, Ramayyan and Nagoji watching Yusuf. Inset, tight, drawn inside this panel's own frame: the scribe's pen at the end of Yusuf's table making one tiny change to a figure, the marks too small to read.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: The king's tax sits between them.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: Too high, the Marakkar captain goes to another coast. Too low, the palace cannot buy Dutch guns to shoot back at Dutch ships.

panels.description: The edge of the market, the last awnings behind them. Ramayyan and Nagoji stepping out onto a firm flat track, Ramayyan musing as he walks. Ahead, the coastal fort: a Travancore fort of red laterite walls and sloping tiled gatehouse roofs, no European flag.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: A diwan who hears only petitions in the court knows half a kingdom.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: The other half lives here, in the way people say 'our pepper' and 'the king's pepper,' as if they are the same, or as if they are not.

panels.description: Wide. The training ground on a flat strip inland from the fort. Men in white stand in lines two deep, matchlocks on their shoulders. The drill master: a stocky, short, older European in a 1740s coat of faded, stained brown (long-skirted, deep cuffs; not red, not Dutch blue), knee breeches, bare-headed, grizzled dark hair tied back, stubble, belly soft, eyes wary. He has turned from the front rank toward Ramayyan and Nagoji, his greeting grin souring into a scowl.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Not De Lannoy. Not yet.

copy.speaker: DRILL MASTER
copy.text: Ram, my friend! You come to see how well they march?

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: I come to see whether they can do more than march.

copy.speaker: DRILL MASTER
copy.text: One thing at a time. First they learn left from right.

panels.description: Wide, the loudest panel in the chapter. The front rank seen side-on, firing as one across the frame toward off-panel right: muzzle flashes along the line, a white sheet of smoke rolling away from camera across the ground. The drill master at the near flank of the line, well clear of the muzzles, arm flung down, mouth open on the word of command. Ramayyan and Nagoji at the left edge, behind the line.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: The smell of saltpetre and burned powder wrapped itself around us.

panels.description: The smoke thinning. Ramayyan, entirely unmoved. Nagoji (clean-shaven chin, thick moustache) looking at him sidelong.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: Adequate.

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: Praise indeed.

panels.description: Ramayyan turning to Nagoji as the line reloads behind them.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: Our men must learn this European dance, or they will die confused when the Dutch play their drums.

panels.description: Wide. A maze of narrow channels and broad lagoons, palm fronds and sky reflected in shards on the water. Boats everywhere: small ones poled by one or two men, broad low ones piled with sacks. On a narrow quay in the foreground, Ibrahim Marakkar (shorter than the boatmen but broader; white turban, short grey-flecked beard; scar from his ANATOMICAL LEFT ear to the jaw, on the camera's right when he faces the viewer; short coat over a vest with bulging pockets) shouting at a boatman heaving one barrel too many aboard.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Here the kingdom's veins opened.

copy.speaker: IBRAHIM
copy.text: Do you want to sit on them? If the boat sinks, the fish will have a feast and the Dutch will laugh.

panels.description: Ibrahim breaking off as he sees Ramayyan and Nagoji arrive, touching his forehead in greeting. Three-quarter view with his anatomical left cheek toward the camera, so the scar from ear to jaw reads.

copy.speaker: IBRAHIM
copy.text: Diwanji. Sawant. Come to see how your horses eat?

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: Horses do not like water. I admire anyone who rides it as if it were a road.

panels.description: Ibrahim grinning, one arm swept out over the lagoon, his scarred anatomical left side toward the camera. On the far bank, small and distant, a low whitewashed Dutch bastion flying a plain red, white and blue banded flag with no monogram or lettering; never a British flag.

copy.speaker: IBRAHIM
copy.text: Water is a road. A road no company can draw a line through.

copy.speaker: IBRAHIM
copy.text: They can put forts on the banks, but the backwaters go where they wish.

panels.description: Ramayyan resting his hand on one of the barrels. Ibrahim at his shoulder.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: Pepper.

copy.speaker: IBRAHIM
copy.text: And a little cardamom. Enough to flavour a Dutchman's breath and his profits.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: And for the king?

panels.description: Ibrahim, hand on his heart, mock-wounded, his scarred anatomical left side toward the camera. Ramayyan's eyes crinkling at the edges.

copy.speaker: IBRAHIM
copy.text: His share is already in his godowns.

copy.speaker: IBRAHIM
copy.text: I am not fool enough to cheat the man whose scribes have longer memories than my own mother.

panels.description: Leaving the quay in late gold light, Ramayyan and Nagoji on a bund between paddy and water. Ramayyan talks without looking at him, the palm-leaf bundle under his arm.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: Horses carry men to battle. Boats carry the coin that pays for their feed.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: Temples carry the stories that make those men willing to die. Markets carry the arguments over who deserves what.

panels.description: Wide and high. From the climbing path, the whole day's country laid out below in the westering sun: the hill temple, the market awnings, the drill ground, the backwaters. The paths between them catch the light like threads. The fort is on the ridge above and behind the viewer, not in the view below: only the edge of its red laterite wall cuts into the top of the frame. Nagoji small in the foreground, looking down at the country.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: In Pune, the world had been simple. Orders came. Men rode. Villages paid. Priests blessed.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Here, everything tied to everything else. A temple roof and a musket barrel and a pepper vine, all tugging on the same knot.

panels.description: The sea appearing beyond the inlet, a flat line of grey and blue. At a turn in the path Nagoji has stopped and is looking back down at the country. Ramayyan, a step ahead and higher on the path, has turned back to him.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: For the Maharaja, conquest is not only taking land. It is knitting these pieces together, so that when a Dutch cannon fires at one place, the rest does not unravel.

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: He is already at war. Even when the Dutch have not fired.

panels.description: Ramayyan, close, glancing up toward the fort above them. Three small insets strung along the bottom of the panel, drawn inside this panel's own frame, in a dark, desaturated tone: a bowman crouched on a palace roof; a hand tipping a vial into a lamp's oil; a dagger half drawn in a festival crowd. No victims shown.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: He has been at war since before he took the throne.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: The Lords of the Eight Houses. The temple yogakkar who thought the gods answered only to them. They sent assassins as often as petitions.

panels.description: Ramayyan and Nagoji walking on, the fort's wall high above them now, dusk coming in off the sea. Ramayyan taps the palm-leaf bundle once and tucks it back under his arm, the way a clerk closes a ledger.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: Only after those knots were cut could he reach outward. Toward Kayamkulam. Then toward Dutch cannon.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: Men like you feel war when the drums beat. Men like him feel it when the accounts do not balance.

panels.description: Dusk at the coastal hall. Through the open doorway, men sit over palm leaves and cups of buttermilk, lamps just lit. Ramayyan has paused on the threshold and turned back to Nagoji.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: You have a sharp eye, Sawant. You see angles on a battlefield. See these angles too.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: When the time comes, the Maharaja will expect you to ride in ways that suit them. Not only your own.

panels.description: Nagoji, his hand resting on the hilt of his talwar. Thick curled moustache, clean-shaven chin, small gold ear stud.

copy.speaker: NAGOJI
copy.text: He has my sword. My eyes he can borrow when he asks.

panels.description: Ramayyan regarding him for a long moment, as if tasting the answer. Half turned toward the lamplit hall.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: Borrowed eyes.

copy.speaker: RAMAYYAN
copy.text: We will see how long he keeps the loan.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: That was the first lesson. The application came soon after.

panels.description: Wide, one frame split into three vertical bands that flow into each other, left to right: riders fording a swollen river in driving rain; a dusty column climbing a northern pass under a hard sun; horses belly deep in monsoon mud, riders hauling at the bridles. Nagoji in each band.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: The months blurred into seasons, the seasons into years.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: In those years, the King turned his 'borrowed eyes' inward, as Ramayyan had promised.

panels.description: A chieftain's gate. Padmini Amma (in her fifties, thick black hair coiled at the nape, simple gold, cotton sari hitched for walking, long walking stick) speaking to the chieftain on his own threshold: a heavy-set, middle-aged Nair lord in red-bordered cloth, gold rings in his ears. An empty bullock cart waits in the road for the levy grain. Nagoji stands silent by the gatepost. Behind him, filling the road, fifty mounted Maravar lancers: white mundus hitched for riding, short jackets, small light ponies, lances upright.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: A campaign in Travancore did not always mean a pitched battle.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: My presence, and the fifty Maravar lancers behind me, turned a request into a requirement.

copy.speaker: CAPTION (separate, weighted)
copy.text: Other times, it was sharper.

panels.description: Wide. Dawn, blue mist. A madampi's estate: high old walls pressed round by thick groves of bamboo. On the wall, one watchman, yawning.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: A madampi near Attingal refused to send his men for the new army drills. He thought his high walls and thick bamboo would protect him from a young King's decrees.

panels.description: Low and fast, inside the bamboo: Maravar horsemen bursting through the wet stems at a gallop, Nagoji at their head, talwar drawn. Inset, tight, drawn inside this panel's own frame: a palm leaf in Ramayyan's hand, the estate's supply paths scratched into it with a stylus as lines only, no lettering.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: He did not know that Ramayyan had mapped his supply lines.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Or that I had trained Maravar horsemen to cut through bamboo dampness as if it were dry grass.

panels.description: High and wide, distance instead of detail: the estate gate broken open, riders inside the walls, the defenders' spears thrown down in the dirt, smoke rising from a burning outbuilding. No bodies. No blood.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: There was no glory in it. Only the brutal efficiency of state-building.

panels.description: The smoking courtyard of an old noble house: carved wooden pillars, a tiled roof scorched at one corner, ash drifting. Marthanda Varma (V13 face; a cream-and-gold turban with its jewelled peacock-feather crest, cream and gold, gold necklaces, bare-chested, spear grounded) standing. Before him the defeated chief: a lean, grey-haired, older Nair lord in fine but disordered white. His sword is still thrust through the waist sash at his side, one hand on its hilt, his eyes on the King. The choice is not yet made. Nagoji at the King's shoulder.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: A house that had been noble for three centuries.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: The King offered its chief a choice. Total submission, or total erasure.

panels.description: Riding back along a wet road, the column behind them. Varma beside Nagoji, both streaked with ash.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: The chief chose submission. His sons marched with us the next week.

copy.speaker: VARMA
copy.text: You see? I do not destroy them because I hate them.

copy.speaker: VARMA
copy.text: I break them so they can be reset into a stronger bone.

panels.description: An evening meal in the barracks. Boots set in a row by the door. Nair soldiers and Maravar riders sit barefoot in a row on the floor mat, rice on plantain leaves. Nagoji among them, barefoot, eating neatly with his right hand: thick curled moustache, clean-shaven chin, rust-red turban. The soldier beside him laughing at something Nagoji has just said.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Somewhere in those years I stopped being a guest and became a limb of this growing beast.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: I learned to distinguish the sullen silence of a conquered village from the quiet respect of a protected one.

panels.description: Narrow strip, tight. A young Nair recruit at dusk ramming a charge down a musket barrel, the ramrod mid-stroke.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: And I learned that peace here was just a word for the time it took to reload.

panels.description: Night at the estate. Nagoji alone, seated among the roots of a great jackfruit tree. Across the yard, lamplight and moving figures in the kalari; far off on its hill, the temple lit.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: By the time the Dutch began to show their teeth, I had ridden every road in the kingdom twice, and forgotten the Deccan hills except in dreams.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Temple to market. Market to fort. Fort to palace. Palace to houses like Padmini's. Houses to Velinadu's halls.

panels.description: Close. Nagoji's left forearm resting on his knee, sleeve pushed back: the Portuguese brand, a pale puckered patch of raised ridges blurred past reading, no letters or numerals, and beside it the long white scar from Chapter 9. The nails healed but ridged. Nothing on the wrist where the iron once was.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: In Goa, chains had held me still in one place.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Here, invisible cords tied me to many. If one snapped, I had no doubt the others would tighten.

panels.description: Wide, full width, final. From the estate's rise at night: the dark kingdom laid out below, pinpricks of lamps at the hill temple, the fort, the market, the backwaters and the palace, and far inland a single lit hall standing apart from the rest, all joined by the faint pale lines of roads. Beyond them the sea, black. Far out on it, a single ship's lantern, too far to name. No figures.

copy.speaker: CAPTION
copy.text: Travancore was already at war, even in its quiet moments. It had just learned to fight with more than swords.

copy.speaker: CAPTION (separate, weighted)
copy.text: If I wished to survive, I would have to learn the same.
